web_title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain, Pricing & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: How a Rupee Flows — Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
question: How does Yash sell into utilities and OEMs, where are its supply-chain bottlenecks, and what does the audited FY26 unit-economics waterfall reveal?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is an engineering vanity metric until it clears working capital and turns into operating cash.
epigraph.author: Industrial Capital Allocation Rule

web_blocks.html: Yash sells through two B2B channels: Transformer OEMs and Direct Utilities/EPCs [1]. It serves 300+ global OEMs and over 1,000 utility customers across 60+ countries, including every Indian state utility and nuclear plant [1]. Utilities dictate approved bushing vendors inside their transformer tenders. Winning an OEM order therefore requires direct end-utility type-test approval, which takes 8 to 10 years [1]. Once approved, switching costs remain high and Yash retains a 96%+ repeat order rate [1].

Abroad, Yash pairs local technical reps with established grid distributors instead of building costly branches. In Europe and North Africa, Weidmann Electrical Technology AG exclusively represents Yash's OIP bushings (up to 245 kV) and HC units (up to 25 kA) [16]. In the United States—home to over 3,000 utilities—Yash HV USA Inc. signed 36-month deals with three regional partners [5]. These include ENSALES Electrical Associates (19 states), Gateway Power Sales (3 Midwestern states), and EHV Solutions LLC (5 Western/South-Central states) [5]. Together, they give Yash sales coverage across 27 US states as of October 2026 [5].

web_blocks.title: 3.2 Supply Chain, Import Dependency & Working Capital Cycle

web_blocks.html: Yash's bill of materials relies on electrical kraft and crepe paper, aluminum foil, epoxy resin, insulators, and copper or aluminum conductors. Historically, its biggest supply-chain bottleneck has been imported RIP capacitive cores [1]. Over 95% of RIP cores assembled in India come from Europe and China [1]. That dependency creates 12-to-16-week lead times, higher freight costs, import duties, and currency exposure [1].

That bottleneck explains why FY26 Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) trailed PAT. Revenue jumped 57% to ₹235.1 crore, so Yash raised buffer inventory from ₹29.7 crore (Mar-25) to ₹66.7 crore (Mar-26) [1][2]. That build pushed the FY26 Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) to 81 days and absorbed ₹51.9 crore in working capital [1][2]. By H1 FY27, inventory stabilized at ₹71.8 crore on a ₹389 crore annualized run-rate [2]. Higher customer advances compressed the CCC to 63 days, even as DSO rose temporarily from 47 to 66 days on Q2 billings [2]. Indigenous RIP/RIS core winding at Jarod in H2 FY27 will remove import duties and shorten lead times [1].

The waterfall below traces Yash Highvoltage's audited FY26 consolidated income statement [1]. It follows ₹235.1 crore of revenue down to ₹37.4 crore of Profit After Tax [1]. It also reconciles earnings to ₹8.82 crore of operating cash flow and ₹59.2 crore of greenfield capex [1].

web_blocks.title: 3.4 Pricing Power, Cost Structure & Operating Leverage

web_blocks.html: Yash's pricing is order-driven and backed by technical specs rather than spot commodities. Utility bushings have long lead times, and the ₹760 crore order book spans 15 to 20 months [1][2]. Yash quotes fixed or formula-adjusted prices that protect raw-material spreads and capture mix gains [1][2]. In FY26, material COGS took 53.3% of revenue (₹125.4 Cr on ₹235.1 Cr) [1]. Employee and direct labor costs took 11.2% (₹26.3 Cr), and other operating expenses took 12.3% (₹28.9 Cr) [1]. Operating EBITDA reached ₹54.5 Cr, or ₹60.4 Cr including ₹5.8 Cr of other income [1].

In H1 FY27, gross margin jumped +590 bps YoY from 42.4% to 48.3% (₹93.9 Cr on ₹194.5 Cr revenue) [1]. Employee costs fell from 11.2% (FY26) to 10.8% of revenue (₹21.0 Cr incl. direct labor) [1]. Other expenses settled at 13.6% (₹26.5 Cr incl. direct mfg), lifting EBITDA margin to 28.1% [1]. Once indigenous RIP core production scales at Jarod, Yash eliminates third-party core margins and import duties [1]. That localization adds another structural gross-margin buffer [1].

Localization also improves working-capital velocity. Importing RIP cores from Europe and China forces 12-to-16-week transit buffers whenever order intake spikes [1]. Producing those cores in Vadodara shortens lead times and lowers work-in-progress inventory. Lower transit stock should help keep the Cash Conversion Cycle below 70 days as revenue scales [2].

book_paragraphs: If you want to know how a specialized industrial company actually makes money, follow two trails: who controls the specification sheet, and where the cash gets stuck between the factory gate and the bank account.

On the specification sheet, Yash sits in an enviable position. Even when a transformer manufacturer like CG Power or Hitachi Energy is building the transformer, the end customer—say, Power Grid Corporation or NTPC—dictates which bushing vendors are approved on the tender. Getting onto that approved vendor list takes eight to ten years of field testing and zero-defect performance. Once you are on it, however, transformer OEMs rarely switch to save a few percentage points on a component that represents a small fraction of the transformer's cost. That is why Yash's repeat order rate sits above 96%.

On the supply-chain trail, however, Yash has had one glaring structural vulnerability: its reliance on imported RIP capacitive cores from Europe and China. When you import the heart of your flagship product, you carry 12 to 16 weeks of shipping lead time, pay import duties, and hold extra buffer inventory whenever global freight tightens. You can see that exact friction in the FY26 numbers: Yash earned ₹37.4 crore in net profit on ₹235.1 crore of revenue, yet operating cash flow was only ₹8.82 crore because inventory more than doubled from ₹29.7 crore to ₹66.7 crore.

book_subsections.title: Reading the Cash Conversion Turnaround in H1 FY27
paragraphs: What separates a disciplined operator from an inventory-bloated manufacturer is what happens next. In H1 FY27, even as revenue surged 95% year-on-year to ₹194.5 crore, Yash held inventory nearly flat at ₹71.8 crore, brought its cash conversion cycle down from 81 days to 63 days, and generated ₹45.2 crore in operating cash flow—125% of net profit.

Now watch what happens as the Jarod greenfield facility commissions in the second half of FY27. By winding and impregnating RIP/RIS cores in-house rather than importing them, Yash removes import duties, air/sea freight, and months of transit inventory in a single stroke—while enabling RIP exports to Europe and the Americas for the first time.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: The FY26 CFO dip to ₹8.82 crore was a working-capital growth tax, not earnings fragility—proven when H1 FY27 CFO snapped back to ₹45.2 crore. Still, keep a close eye on receivable days, which ticked up from 47 to 66 days in H1 FY27.

book_subsections.title: Why Localization at Jarod Changes Both Margins and Working Capital
paragraphs: To understand the strategic logic of the ₹220 crore Jarod greenfield plant, put yourself in the shoes of Yash's procurement head over the past five years. When more than 95% of India's RIP capacitive cores are imported from Europe and China, every surge in domestic demand forces you to place core orders 12 to 16 weeks in advance, pay air or ocean freight, absorb customs duties, and sit on elevated work-in-progress inventory.

Worse still, you cannot competitively export RIP bushings to Europe or North America if you are buying the core from Europe, flying it to Gujarat, assembling it, and shipping it back out. By installing Swiss and German winding and resin-impregnation lines inside Jarod—with Phase 1 assembly already generating its first invoice in H1 FY27 and full end-to-end core production commissioning in Q3 FY27—Yash turns a supply-chain bottleneck into a cost and lead-time advantage.

book_subsections.title: Distribution Leverage: Why Partnering Beats Building Direct Sales Forces
paragraphs: Look at how Yash approaches international distribution. Rather than hiring dozens of salaried salespeople across Europe and the United States—which would bloat fixed SG&A ahead of revenue—Yash partnered with Weidmann Electrical Technology AG in Europe and North Africa, and built a commission-aligned representation network across 27 US states through ENSALES Electrical Associates, Gateway Power Sales, and EHV Solutions LLC.

That structure keeps fixed overhead low while putting Yash's technical catalog in front of more than 3,000 American utilities through local engineers who already know the regional utility buyers. As US and European orders convert from homologation into recurring shipments in FY28, the incremental operating leverage flows straight to EBITDA.
